title-group.article-title: The efficacy and safety of ticagrelor and prasugrel versus clopidogrel in post-PCI dual antiplatelet therapy in chronic coronary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Clopidogrel is the guideline-recommended P2Y12 inhibitor for dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in Chronic Coronary Syndrome (CCS). Recent evidence suggests potential benefits of more potent P2Y12 inhibitors, primarily Ticagrelor, though their role in CCS remains less defined than in acute settings.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To compare the efficacy and safety of Ticagrelor or Prasugrel with Clopidogrel in DAPT following PCI in CCS patients.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systematic approach was used to identify eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies comparing the safety and efficacy of Ticagrelor or Prasugrel versus Clopidogrel. A meta-analysis using a random-effects model evaluated major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), its individual components, and bleeding outcomes. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Subgroup analyses were performed by study design, P2Y12 inhibitor type, follow-up duration, and geographical region.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Twelve studies (6 RCTs, 6 observational) were included, comprising 10,048 patients receiving potent P2Y12 inhibitors (Ticagrelor: 10 studies; Prasugrel: 3 studies) and 45,103 receiving Clopidogrel. Potent P2Y12 inhibitors were associated with a significantly reduced risk of MACE (OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.55–0.88) and all-cause mortality (OR = 0.63, 95% CI: 0.46–0.88). These benefits were primarily driven by the Ticagrelor subgroup, observational data, follow-up > 6 months, and Asian studies. While no significant differences were found for myocardial infarction, stroke, or overall stent thrombosis, the Ticagrelor subgroup showed a significantly lower risk of revascularization (OR = 0.67, 95%CI: 0.52–0.86). Regarding safety, while major bleeding showed a non-significant trend toward increase (OR = 1.41, 95% CI: 0.92–2.17), minor bleeding was significantly higher in the potent P2Y12 group (OR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.26–1.95).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta-analysis suggests that intensified DAPT, primarily Ticagrelor-based, may offer superior clinical benefit to Clopidogrel-based DAPT in patients with CCS undergoing PCI, particularly by reducing MACE, all-cause mortality, and revascularization. However, these benefits are accompanied by an increased risk of minor bleeding and a potential signal toward higher major bleeding. Considering the scarcity of large-scale RCTs, heterogeneous MACE definitions, limited data on Prasugrel, and ethnic/racial influence on bleeding risk and thrombotic events, these findings emphasize the need for individualized post-PCI antiplatelet regimens and support further long-term RCTs to better define the role of potent P2Y12 inhibitors in this population.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) represents the most frequent indication for coronary angiography and subsequent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) [1]. Despite advances in interventional techniques, PCI is still associated with an increased risk of thrombotic complications, particularly due to mechanical disruption of atherosclerotic plaques, which can lead to platelet activation and aggregation [2]. To mitigate this risk and prevent adverse ischemic outcomes, including reinfarction, current guidelines recommend the routine use of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), a combination of aspirin and a P2Y12 receptor inhibitor, following PCI [3].

For many years, clopidogrel remained the cornerstone P2Y12 receptor inhibitor in DAPT [4]. However, the emergence of more potent P2Y12 inhibitors such as ticagrelor and prasugrel has led to a paradigm shift in the treatment of acute coronary syndromes (ACS) [3, 5, 6]. Ticagrelor, a direct-acting and reversible agent, achieves rapid and consistent platelet inhibition without the need for metabolic activation [7]. Prasugrel, although requiring hepatic conversion, binds irreversibly and delivers a stronger and more sustained antiplatelet effect [8]. Nonetheless, clopidogrel remains the guideline-recommended P2Y12 inhibitor for patients with CCS, largely due to the overall lower risk profile typically associated with this population [5]. Despite this, real-world practice patterns suggest a growing trend toward off-label use of ticagrelor and prasugrel, especially in Asian countries [9]. Yet, this evolving practice warrants further rigorous evaluation. While intensified platelet inhibition may confer additional ischemic protection, it also raises important concerns regarding increased bleeding risk, reduced medication adherence, and greater financial burden associated with the newer agents [10, 11].

Although randomized trials have been conducted to compare clopidogrel with newer P2Y12 inhibitors in CCS patients undergoing PCI, the available evidence is limited by demographic constraints, variations in inclusion criteria, short follow-up durations, and differences in study regions that affect racial composition. Many studies were underpowered to detect meaningful differences or were not designed to assess superiority, and some were terminated prematurely [12–15]. These limitations hinder the generalizability of findings and leave important questions unanswered. To address these gaps, we conducted a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of clopidogrel versus ticagrelor and prasugrel in the context of DAPT following PCI for CCS.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the 2020 PRISMA guidelines and was prospectively registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD420251016174).

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: A comprehensive search strategy was developed using core keywords such as “Clopidogrel”, “Prasugrel”, and “Ticagrelor” in combination with terms related to "Chronic Coronary Syndrome" and major cardiovascular outcomes. The search terms included both MeSH headings and free-text synonyms to ensure broad coverage of relevant literature.

We systematically searched the following electronic databases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL, covering all records available through January 1, 2025. The search strings targeted both the drug names and condition-specific terminology such as “chronic coronary syndrome,” “stable angina,” “percutaneous coronary intervention,” and “major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).” Full search strategy and detailed queries for each database are provided in the Supplementary Material.

To enhance the comprehensiveness of the review, grey literature was also explored through manual screening of Google Scholar, backward citation tracking of included articles, and review of relevant systematic reviews.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: Studies were selected based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria structured according to the PICO framework. The population of interest included adult patients (≥ 18 years of age) diagnosed with CCS who had undergone elective PCI. The intervention (case) group received maintenance DAPT comprising Aspirin plus either Ticagrelor or Prasugrel, while the comparison (control) group received Aspirin plus Clopidogrel as maintenance therapy.

The primary outcomes assessed were the incidence of MACE, defined according to the primary composite endpoint specified in each study. These composites generally included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospitalization for heart failure, and the need for revascularization. Additionally, the incidence of major bleeding events, classified as BARC types 3 to 5 or TIMI major, was included as a co-primary safety outcome. Secondary outcomes comprised the individual components of the MACE composite and the incidence of minor bleeding events (defined as BARC types 1 to 2 or TIMI minor) during the follow-up period.

Eligible studies were required to be randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or observational studies comparing the specified maintenance DAPT regimens, with a minimum follow-up duration of one month and reporting at least one predefined primary or secondary outcome among CCS patients. For studies involving mixed clinical presentations of ACS and CCS, inclusion was contingent upon the availability of discrete outcome data for the CCS subgroup. Data extraction was limited strictly to the CCS cohorts to ensure the homogeneity of the study population. Exclusion criteria encompassed case reports, case series, editorials, studies evaluating only loading doses of P2Y12 inhibitors without maintenance therapy, studies with follow-up shorter than one month, and those lacking data on relevant clinical outcomes.

sec.title: Study selection and data extraction
sec.p: The search results were initially imported into EndNote for duplicate removal. The remaining unique citations were then uploaded to Rayyan for title and abstract screening. Four independent reviewers (MA, HY, AM, and MB) conducted the initial screening to identify potentially eligible studies. Each of the studies deemed relevant or requiring further assessment was retrieved and evaluated against the inclusion criteria by two of these reviewers. Any disagreements regarding study inclusion were resolved through discussion between the reviewers, and when necessary, a Fifth reviewer (SAM) was consulted to reach consensus.

Data extraction was carried out independently by two authors using a predefined and pilot-tested data extraction form to ensure consistency and minimize bias. The following information was extracted from each study: author name, year of publication, country of study, and study design; sample sizes for each treatment arm; baseline patient characteristics including age and sex distribution; duration of follow-up; type of P2Y12 inhibitor used and the dosing regimen; and all reported clinical outcomes of interest, including components of MACE and bleeding events classified by BARC and TIMI criteria.

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: Given that the included studies comprised both RCTs and observational designs, we applied two distinct tools to assess the risk of bias accordingly. For RCTs, the Risk of Bias 2 (ROB-2) tool, developed by Cochrane, was employed. This tool evaluates potential bias across five domains and classifies studies as having a low risk of bias, some concerns, or a high risk of bias [16, 17]. In contrast, for non-randomized studies, we used the ROBINS-I (Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions) tool [18]. This framework assesses bias in areas such as confounding factors, participant selection, intervention classification, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and reporting. Based on this assessment, studies were categorized into one of four levels: low, moderate, serious, or critical risk of bias.

sec.title: Quantitative analysis
sec.p: We conducted all quantitative analyses using a random-effects meta-analysis model, employing the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimator to account for inter-study variability. For dichotomous outcomes, such as MACE and bleeding events, pooled effect sizes were expressed as odds ratios (ORs), each with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). This approach allowed for the synthesis of results across studies with differing sample sizes and effect estimates.

Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic and the Chi-squared test. The subgroup analyses were conducted based on study design (RCTs vs. observational studies), the specific P2Y12 inhibitor used (Ticagrelor vs. Prasugrel), duration of follow-up (1–6 months vs. over 6 months), and geographical region (Asian vs. non-Asian). Publication bias was assessed using funnel plot inspection and Egger’s regression test for outcomes with more than 10 included studies. All statistical procedures were carried out using Stata version 17, with a two-tailed p-value of < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A comprehensive search of databases identified 7,564 studies. Following the removal of duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, 55 studies were selected for full-text review. Of these, a total of 12 studies were included in the final analysis, comprising six RCTs [19–24] and six observational studies [25–30]. Figure 1 depicts the study selection process.

Overall population included in the case group is 10,048 participants (18.22%) and 45,103 (81.78%) in the control group. The mean ages of participants in the case and control groups were 61.05 and 61.53 years, respectively. Male participants accounted for 77.08% of the case group and 75.02% of the control group. With respect to follow-up duration, three studies had a 1-month follow-up period [19, 21, 29], Two studies followed participants for 6 months [20, 24], Six studies had a 12-month follow-up [23, 25–28, 30], and one study reported outcomes at 24 months [22]. Regarding the type of P2Y12 inhibitor used in the case group, one study used both Ticagrelor and Prasugrel [30], nine studies only used Ticagrelor [19–22, 25–29], and two studies only used Prasugrel [23, 24]. The details regarding baseline characteristics of studies were summarized in Table 1.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: Among the six included RCTs, four out of six studies revealed low risk of concern [19, 21, 22, 24]; however, the remaining two studies showed some concern [20, 23]. Risks were mostly related to the selection of reported results and missing of outcomes domains (Supplementary Table 1). For the six observational studies, quality assessment using the ROBINS-I tool indicated low risk of bias in two studies [26, 30] and moderate risk in four studies [25, 27–29]. Most of the risks were related to the domain of confounding (Supplementary Table 2).

sec.title: MACE
sec.p: As illustrated in Fig. 2, pooled analysis of 11 studies demonstrated a significantly lower risk of MACE in patients receiving potent P2Y12 inhibitors compared with clopidogrel (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55; 0.88, I2 = 44.3%, p-heterogeneity = 0.043). The subgroup analyses stratified by P2Y12 inhibitor, study design, and follow-up duration showed directionally concordant reductions in MACE incidence compared with the main analysis, although only the studies with ticagrelor as P2Y12 inhibitor, observational design, and follow-up duration > 6 months reached statistical significance. Stratification by geographical region demonstrated a significant benefit of potent P2Y12 inhibitors in Asian populations, while this effect was not observed in non-Asian cohorts. Detailed subgroup results are provided in the Supplementary Materials (Supplementary Table 3–4 and Supplementary Fig. 1–9).

caption.p: The main and subgroup meta-analyses comparing major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in potent P2Y12 inhibitors (ticagrelor or prasugrel) versus clopidogrel in dual antiplatelet therapy following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS)

sec.title: All-cause and cardiovascular mortality
sec.p: Pooled analysis of seven studies revealed a significant reduction in all-cause mortality in the case group (OR = 0.63, 95% CI 0.46; 0.88, I2 = 0%, p-heterogeneity = 0.714). Subgroup analyses showed consistent reductions across all subgroups. However, statistical significance was achieved only in the ticagrelor, observational study, follow-up > 6 months, and Asian subgroups (Fig. 3-A). Six studies reported cardiovascular mortality. The pooled estimate showed a non-significant trend toward lower cardiovascular mortality with potent P2Y12 inhibition (OR = 0.70, 95% CI 0.48; 1.04, I2 = 0%, p-heterogeneity = 0. 674). Although all subgroup estimates favored potent P2Y12 inhibitors, statistically significant reductions were observed only in RCTs and in studies with follow-up ≤ 6 months (Fig. 3-B).

caption.p: Main and subgroup analyses for all-cause mortality (A) and cardiovascular mortality (B)

sec.title: MI, stroke/TIA, stent thrombosis, and revascularization
sec.p: The incidence of MI was evaluated in eleven studies. The pooled analysis revealed no statistically significant difference in MI risk between the groups (OR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.67; 1.16, I2 = 37.1%, p-heterogeneity = 0.079). Subgroup analyses were largely consistent with the overall estimate, although a significant reduction in MI was observed within the observational studies subgroup. For stroke or TIA, eight studies were included in the analysis. The overall pooled analysis indicated a non-significant trend toward lower risk in the case group (OR = 0.72, 95%CI 0.50; 1.05, I2 = 0%, p-heterogeneity = 0.938). No subgroup demonstrated a statistically significant difference except for observational studies, which showed a significant association with reduced stroke/TIA risk. Regarding the risk of stent thrombosis, six studies were analyzed, and the pooled analysis showed no significant difference between the groups (OR = 0.80, 95% CI 0.49; 1.30, I2 = 0%, p-heterogeneity = 0.875). Subgroup analysis by P2Y12 inhibitor did not show a significant difference in stent thrombosis risk for either Ticagrelor or Prasugrel. However, observational studies, studies with follow-up > 6 months, and those conducted in Asian populations demonstrated significantly lower rates of stent thrombosis. The outcome of revascularization was reported in six studies. The pooled analysis indicated a significantly lower risk in the case group (OR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.52–0.86, I2 = 15%, p-heterogeneity = 0.312). All studies included in the overall analysis used Ticagrelor. Almost all subgroup analyses showed a statistically significant reduction in revascularization risk, whereas RCTs did not demonstrate a significant difference. The results of the main and subgroup analyses for MI, stroke/TIA, stent thrombosis, and revascularization are presented in Fig. 4A-4D, respectively.

caption.p: Main and subgroup analyses for myocardial infarction (A), stroke/TIA (B), stent thrombosis (C), and revascularization (D)

sec.title: Bleeding
sec.p: The pooled analysis of major bleeding, based on seven studies, indicated a non-significant trend toward increased major bleeding risk with more potent P2Y12 inhibitors (OR = 1.41, 95% CI 0.92; 2.17, I2 = 0.1%, p-heterogeneity = 0.428). Subgroup analyses consistently showed no statistically significant associations (Fig. 5A). In contrast, minor bleeding was reported in six studies and was significantly increased among patients receiving ticagrelor (OR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.26–1.95, I2 = 7.5%, p-heterogeneity = 0.372). These findings were consistent across most subgroups, although statistical significance was not reached in studies with follow-up ≤ 6 months or in non-Asian populations (Fig. 5B).

caption.p: Main and subgroup analyses for major bleeding (A) and minor bleeding (B)

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: Visual assessment of funnel plots suggested a moderate degree of asymmetry for most outcomes, indicating a potential risk of publication bias.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence from twelve studies (6 RCTs and 6 observational studies) to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of Ticagrelor- or Prasugrel-based DAPT versus clopidogrel-based DAPT in patients with CCS. The findings revealed that intensified DAPT was associated with a statistically significant reduction in MACE, all-cause mortality, and the need for revascularization. Subgroup analyses highlighted that these benefits were more pronounced in observational studies and among patients receiving Ticagrelor, particularly in studies conducted in Asian countries with longer follow-up durations. Although outcomes such as cardiovascular mortality, MI, stroke/TIA, and stent thrombosis did not consistently reach statistical significance, they generally favored the Ticagrelor/Prasugrel-based regimens over clopidogrel. Importantly, safety analyses indicated a significantly increased risk of minor bleeding events, with a non-significant trend toward increased major bleeding, underscoring the trade-off between ischemic benefit and bleeding risk associated with potent antiplatelet agents. The subgroup analysis of studies assessing Prasugrel and the RCTs did not demonstrate a significant benefit of potent P2Y12 inhibitors over clopidogrel. It is important to note that only three studies evaluated Prasugrel, which limits the reliability and generalizability of conclusions regarding its efficacy. Moreover, the included RCTs, on average, had shorter follow-up durations than observational studies, which may have attenuated the ability to detect differences in long-term ischemic outcomes.

Our findings should be interpreted in the context of prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses examining similar strategies in other populations. Ullah et al. evaluated various DAPT approaches in ACS patients undergoing PCI, including short-term and de-escalated regimens, and found that more potent or hybrid strategies offered better protection against MACE compared to standard clopidogrel [31]. Lee et al. focused on reduced-dose Prasugrel in PCI-treated patients and observed modest MACE reduction relative to clopidogrel, consistent with the limited yet directional benefit seen in our Prasugrel subgroup [32]. Meanwhile, Li et al. found no MACE benefit of Ticagrelor over clopidogrel in East Asian ACS patients, reflecting possible regional variability in ischemic risk and pharmacogenetic response [33]. While these studies focus on ACS or demographically distinct populations, our findings contribute to this body of evidence by specifically focusing on CCS patients, a population underrepresented in previous analyses.

The mortality benefit in our analyses was predominantly observed in the Ticagrelor subgroup. In contrast, the reduction in cardiovascular mortality did not reach statistical significance overall, though a significant association was detected in studies with shorter follow-up durations. This pattern may reflect the timing and nature of mortality events in CCS populations, where early post-procedural cardiovascular deaths are more susceptible to antiplatelet modulation, while non-cardiovascular factors may increasingly influence longer-term mortality. For all-cause mortality, the lack of significant findings in RCTs may be due to the shorter follow-up durations across these studies and the overall low number of mortality events, limiting the statistical power to detect differences. In contrast, observational studies with longer follow-up were more likely to capture late mortality trends, but may also be subject to confounding. For cardiovascular mortality, the significant findings in both RCTs and studies with shorter follow-up reflect a consistent trend, which is consistent with the relatively short follow-up durations of the included randomized trials. While meta-analyses of ACS patients demonstrate promising mortality benefits with Ticagrelor-based DAPT, our findings suggest that these survival advantages may extend beyond the acute setting and into the more stable, yet still vulnerable, CCS population [33–35].

Neither MI nor stroke/TIA showed a statistically significant reduction with Ticagrelor- or Prasugrel-based DAPT compared to clopidogrel in our analysis. While the point estimates for both outcomes numerically favored intensified therapy, the confidence intervals crossed unity, and subgroup analyses largely echoed this pattern. For MI, this lack of statistical significance persisted across all subgroups, suggesting that intensified DAPT may not offer consistent incremental protection against recurrent infarction in the CCS population. This is perhaps unsurprising, as patients with CCS typically present with more stable plaque biology and a lower short-term thrombotic risk than those with ACS, reducing the likelihood of observing large treatment effects. In contrast, the stroke/TIA outcome demonstrated a borderline benefit in some subgroups, including studies evaluating Ticagrelor and those with observational design. However, these associations did not hold across all analyses, and the overall estimate remained non-significant. The modest trend toward stroke reduction may reflect a systemic antiplatelet effect, yet its variability across study types and agents suggests that this outcome may be more sensitive to differences in baseline vascular risk, antiplatelet potency, and treatment adherence. In line with our findings, a network meta-analysis by Liu et al., which included only CCS patients, reported that Ticagrelor added to aspirin significantly reduced MI risk compared to aspirin alone but did not demonstrate superiority over clopidogrel in head-to-head comparisons [36]. Taken together, these findings imply that while intensified DAPT may offer some ischemic protection beyond MACE and mortality, its effect on individual endpoints like MI and stroke appears attenuated in the context of CCS.

We found a significant reduction in the risk of revascularization among patients treated with Ticagrelor-based DAPT compared to clopidogrel, with this benefit consistently observed across different follow-up durations and geographical regions. This finding suggests that intensified platelet inhibition may contribute to a sustained reduction in ischemic recurrences requiring procedural intervention, even in the relatively lower-risk CCS population. The discrepancy between significant observational results and non-significant RCT findings likely reflects the higher anatomical complexity (e.g., high SYNTAX scores) encountered in real-world practice, where the pharmacodynamic advantages of potent P2Y12 inhibitors are most pronounced. In contrast, the outcome of stent thrombosis did not reach statistical significance overall, although favorable trends were noted in subgroups with observational design, longer follow-up, and Asian studies. This regional benefit is likely tied to the "East Asian Paradox"; Asian patients exhibit higher rates of clopidogrel resistance due to CYP2C19 polymorphisms, making the superior, consistent inhibition of ticagrelor or prasugrel more clinically impactful in this demographic compared to Western populations. Additionally, relative studies suggest that potent P2Y₁₂ inhibitors are effective in reducing stent-related events, including the need for revascularization in high-risk settings [34, 37, 38]. The limited number of stent thrombosis events and the inherently low incidence of this complication in CCS patients may account for the lack of statistical power in our analyses. Moreover, while revascularization is often influenced by a combination of clinical symptoms, non-invasive testing, and physician discretion, stent thrombosis represents a more strictly defined and adjudicated outcome, potentially explaining the discrepancy in significance between these two endpoints.

Our analysis revealed a clear safety signal associated with intensified DAPT in the CCS population, with a significantly increased risk of minor bleeding and a non-significant trend toward higher major bleeding. The elevated minor bleeding risk was consistent across study designs, particularly in those with longer than six months of follow-up, suggesting a cumulative risk associated with more potent antiplatelet therapy over time. Although major bleeding did not reach statistical significance overall, the direction of effect and upper confidence bounds raise clinically relevant concerns, especially in stable patients where the ischemic benefit is more modest. Importantly, the bleeding risk appeared similar across study designs and drug subgroups, indicating that this safety concern is likely intrinsic to the pharmacologic profile of Ticagrelor and Prasugrel rather than study-level confounding. Prior studies across ACS and CCS populations have consistently reported elevated bleeding risk with potent P2Y₁₂ inhibitors, echoing the trends observed in our analysis [35, 37–39]. These findings reinforce the need to balance ischemic protection with bleeding risk when considering intensified antiplatelet regimens in CCS, particularly for patients with longer expected treatment durations or higher baseline bleeding risk. Although Ticagrelor or Prasugrel may be better choices for DAPT based on our meta-analysis, recent studies and ongoing trials suggest that P2Y12 monotherapy with these agents could be non-inferior to DAPT with clopidogrel, leaving the debate unresolved [40, 41].

This study has several limitations that warrant consideration. First, while we included both RCTs and observational studies to enhance generalizability, this introduced heterogeneity in study design, follow-up duration, and risk of bias. The observational studies, while informative, were subject to potential confounding and selection bias, and several were rated as having moderate risk of bias. Moreover, the majority of the pooled population was derived from observational cohorts; given that the absolute differences in outcomes between P2Y12 inhibitors are often narrow, the influence of these studies on the final estimates must be acknowledged. Consequently, while our findings provide a clearer trend in the comparative efficacy and safety of these agents, the results of the combined analysis should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive proof of superiority. Second, a significant proportion of the included studies were conducted in Asian populations. It is well-established that patient ethnicity can influence the pharmacodynamics of P2Y12 inhibitors; for instance, East Asian patients frequently exhibit a higher prevalence of CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles, which impacts clopidogrel responsiveness. Furthermore, the 'East Asian Paradox' suggests a different therapeutic window for anticoagulation in these patients compared to Western cohorts. Future global head-to-head RCTs are necessary to confirm these trends across diverse ethnic groups. The third limitation of this meta-analysis is the heterogeneity in the definitions of MACE across the included studies. While some studies defined MACE as a composite of three outcomes, others included additional components such as hospitalization for heart failure or repeat revascularization, which may represent softer endpoints. This variability may have introduced bias and should be considered when interpreting the pooled results. Fourth, only three studies evaluated Prasugrel-based DAPT, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions about its efficacy and safety compared to clopidogrel. Additionally, some outcomes, such as stent thrombosis and cardiovascular mortality, were infrequent across the included trials, reducing statistical power and the reliability of subgroup comparisons. One other limitation of this meta-analysis is the inability to stratify bleeding events according to standardized ARC consensus categories (e.g., major, clinically relevant non-major, or fatal bleeding) due to variability in bleeding definitions and reporting across the included studies. Finally, the relatively short follow-up durations in randomized trials may have further limited the detection of long-term safety and efficacy trends.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis provides evidence that Ticagrelor- or Prasugrel-based DAPT may offer incremental clinical benefit over clopidogrel-based regimens in patients with chronic coronary syndrome undergoing PCI. Specifically, Ticagrelor was associated with reductions in MACE, all-cause mortality, and revascularization, with favorable trends in other ischemic outcomes. However, these benefits were accompanied by an increased risk of minor bleeding and a possible signal toward higher major bleeding. These findings highlight the trade-offs between ischemic protection and bleeding risk in the CCS population and underscore the importance of individualized antiplatelet strategies. Further high-quality, long-term randomized trials are needed to better define the optimal role of potent P2Y₁₂ inhibitors in stable coronary disease, particularly for subgroups at high ischemic or bleeding risk.
